title: 10 facts about U.S. Catholics
summary: Pew Research Center outlines 10 key facts about U.S. Catholics using its 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study and other surveys. About 20% of U.S. adults identify as Catholic (roughly 53 million adults). The population is becoming more Hispanic and immigrant, skews older overall, is regionally dispersed, and shows varied educational attainment, religious practice, and partisan leanings. Major findings include views on abortion and high favorability for Pope Francis.
content:
Pew Research Center presents 10 facts about U.S. Catholics based on the 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study (RLS), the National Public Opinion Reference Survey (NPORS), the American Trends Panel, and earlier telephone surveys.

1) Size and global rank: Catholics are one of the largest religious groups in the United States and outnumber any single Protestant denomination. The U.S. has more Catholics than all but three countries worldwide: Brazil, Mexico and the Philippines (Vatican 2021 Statistical Yearbook).

2) Share of U.S. adults: About 20% of U.S. adults describe themselves as Catholic, a share that has been fairly stable since 2014 but is slightly lower than in 2007 (24%). With roughly 267 million U.S. adults in 2024, this equates to about 53 million Catholic adults.

3) Racial and ethnic composition: The Catholic population is 54% White, 36% Hispanic, 4% Asian and 2% Black, with 2% identifying another race. Since 2007 the share who are White has fallen by 10 percentage points while the Hispanic share has grown by 7 points.

4) Immigration and generation status: Over four-in-ten U.S. Catholics are immigrants (29%) or the children of immigrants (14%). Rates are especially high among Asian Catholics (78% foreign-born) and Hispanic Catholics (58% foreign-born). By contrast, 83% of White Catholics come from families in the U.S. for three generations or longer.

5) Age profile: Catholics tend to be older than the general population: 58% of Catholic adults are age 50 or older, compared with 47% of all U.S. adults in the RLS. But Hispanic and Asian Catholics are younger on average than White Catholics.

6) Regional distribution: Catholics are relatively evenly distributed across regions: 29% live in the South, 26% in the Northeast, 25% in the West and 20% in the Midwest. Racial and ethnic mixes differ by region: the West has a Hispanic plurality among Catholics (58%) and a larger share of Asian Catholics (10%), while the Midwest and Northeast have higher shares of White Catholics.

7) Education: About 35% of U.S. Catholics have a bachelor's degree, 27% have some college but no bachelor's, and 38% have a high school education or less. Educational attainment is higher for Asian and White Catholics than for Hispanic Catholics.

8) Religious practice and importance: Around 29% of Catholics say they attend Mass weekly or more, 51% pray daily, and 44% say religion is very important in their lives. About 21% report attending Mass weekly, praying daily and considering religion very important.

9) Partisanship and political attitudes: Among registered voters who are Catholic, 53% identify with or lean toward the Republican Party and 43% with the Democratic Party. But partisanship varies by race and ethnicity: 61% of White Catholic registered voters lean or identify Republican, while 56% of Hispanic Catholic registered voters lean or identify Democratic.

10) Abortion and views of the pope: Although the Catholic Church opposes abortion, 59% of Catholics say abortion should be legal (35% in most cases, 25% in all cases). Views align with partisan leanings: 78% of Catholic Democrats say abortion should be legal in most or all cases, compared with 43% of Catholic Republicans. About 78% of Catholics view Pope Francis favorably in Pew's February 2025 survey, with higher favorability among Catholic Democrats (88%) than Catholic Republicans (69%).

Methodology note: The analysis draws primarily on the Center's 2023-24 RLS and NPORS, which use address-based sampling and weigh respondents to be representative of the U.S. adult population by gender, race, ethnicity and education. The post also uses the American Trends Panel and earlier random-digit-dial surveys. Some subgroups, such as Black Catholics, were not large enough in the 2023-24 survey to be reported separately.

Authors and source: The piece was prepared by researchers at Pew Research Center and updates an earlier post first published Sept. 4, 2018. Pew Research Center is a nonpartisan, nonadvocacy fact tank based in Washington, D.C.

content.content:
Numbers, Facts and Trends Shaping Your World

Read our research on:

Full Topic List

Read Our Research On:

Religious Landscape Study

|

Catholics are one of the largest religious groups in the United States, outnumbering any single Protestant denomination. The U.S. has more Catholics than all but three other countries – Brazil, Mexico and the Philippines – according to the Vatican’s 2021 Statistical Yearbook of the Church.

Here are 10 key facts about the U.S. Catholic population, drawn from Pew Research Center surveys.

Pew Research Center conducted this analysis to explore the basic demographic traits, religious characteristics and political preferences of U.S. Catholics.

The analysis draws mainly on data from the Center’s2023-24 Religious Landscape Study (RLS). It also draws from the Center’sNational Public Opinion Reference Survey (NPORS), an annual benchmarking survey of U.S. adults. Both the RLS and NPORS use address-based sampling from the U.S. Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File to recruit participants. RLS respondents were surveyed mainly online or on paper, though respondents also had the option of calling a toll-free number to participate by telephone. NPORS respondents could answer either by paper or online. Follow the links to read more about each survey’s methodology.

This post also relies on online surveys of respondents who are part of the Center’sAmerican Trends Panel. Data from before 2020 comes from the Center’s random-digit-dial telephone surveys.

All of these surveys are weighted to be representative of the U.S. adult population by gender, race, ethnicity, education and other categories.

Today, 20% of U.S. adults describe themselves as Catholics.This percentage has been generally stable since 2014. But it is slightly lower than in 2007, when 24% of U.S. adults identified as Catholic.

Overall, there were about 267 million U.S. adults in 2024,according to the U.S. Census Bureau. This suggests that there are roughly 53 million Catholic adults nationwide.

The share of U.S. Catholics who are Hispanic is rising.Currently, the Catholic population is 54% White, 36% Hispanic, 4% Asian and 2% Black. An additional 2% identify with another race.

Since 2007, the share who are White has dropped by 10 percentage points, while the share who are Hispanic has grown by 7 points.

This change has implications for the profile of Catholic Americans overall because Catholics from different racial and ethnic backgrounds have distinctive social and political traits, as we’ll discuss below.

More than four-in-ten U.S. Catholics are immigrants (29%) or the children of immigrants (14%).But some racial and ethnic groups have much higher shares of first- and second-generation immigrants.

For example, 78% of Asian Catholics were born outside the U.S., and an additional 14% were born in the U.S. but have at least one parent who was not.

Among Hispanic Catholics, 58% were born outside the U.S., and 22% were born in the U.S. to at least one immigrant parent.

By contrast, 83% of White Catholics are from families who have been in the U.S. for three generations or longer.

(The 2023-24 survey did not include enough Black Catholics to report on them separately. Refer to our2022 analysisfor more information about Black Catholics.)

Catholics tend to be older than Americans overall.Nearly six-in-ten Catholic adults (58%) are ages 50 and older. By comparison, 47% ofallU.S. adults in the Center’s2023-24 Religious Landscape Study (RLS)fall in this age range.

But Hispanic Catholics and Asian Catholics tend to be a lot younger than White Catholics. Four-in-ten Hispanic Catholics and 53% of Asian Catholics are 50 and older, compared with 70% of White Catholics. And just 14% of Hispanic Catholics and 20% of Asian Catholics are ages 65 and older, versus 39% of White Catholics.

Catholics are spread out relatively evenly across the U.S.Roughly three-in-ten (29%) live in the South, while 26% live in the Northeast, 25% in the West and 20% in the Midwest.

The racial and ethnic makeup of the Catholic population varies by region. For example, in the Midwest, 78% of Catholics are White and 15% are Hispanic. In the Northeast, 72% of Catholics are White and 20% are Hispanic.

In the South, 44% are White and 45% are Hispanic. And in the West, there are more Hispanic Catholics than White Catholics (58% vs. 27%). The West also has a relatively larger population of Asian Catholics than do other regions (10%).

More than one-third of U.S. Catholics (35%) have a bachelor’s degree.Another 27% have some college experience but not a bachelor’s degree, and 38% have a high school education or less. This distribution is similar to that of the general adult population.

On average, Asian Catholics and White Catholics have higher levels of educational attainment than Hispanic Catholics. About half of Asian Catholics (53%) have a college degree, while 21% have a high school education or less. Among White Catholics, 43% have at least a bachelor’s degree, while 29% have a high school education or less. Among Hispanic Catholics, 20% have a bachelor’s degree and 54% have a high school education or less.

About three-in-ten U.S. Catholics (29%) say they attend Mass weekly or more often.Larger shares say they pray on a daily basis (51%) and say religion is very important in their lives (44%). By comparison, Protestants are slightly more likely to say they do or believe each of these things.

Overall, 21% of U.S. Catholics say they attend Mass weeklyandpray dailyandconsider religion very important. By contrast, 10% say they attend Mass a few times a year or less, pray seldom or never,andconsider religion not too or not all important.

About half of Catholics who are registered voters (53%) identify with or lean toward the Republican Party, while 43% affiliate with the Democratic Party.

But partisan affiliation varies by race and ethnicity. Roughly six-in-ten White Catholic registered voters (61%) say they identify with or lean toward the GOP, while 36% identify with or lean toward the Democratic Party.

Conversely, 56% of Hispanic Catholics who are registered voters say they identify with or lean toward the Democratic Party, compared with 39% who favor the GOP.

While theCatholic Church opposes abortion, 59% of Catholics say abortion should be legal.This includes 35% who say it should be legal in most cases and 25% who say it should be legal in all cases. Roughly four-in-ten Catholics say abortion should beillegalin most (26%) or all (13%) cases.

Catholics’ opinions about abortion tend to align with their political leanings. Among Catholic Democrats, 78% say abortion should be legal in most or all cases. Among Catholic Republicans, 43% say this.

Catholic Democrats (78%) are a little less likely than Democrats as a whole (86%) to say abortion should be legal in most or all cases.

Roughly three-quarters of Catholics (78%) view Pope Francis favorably,according toour February 2025 survey. At least 80% of Catholics have expressed a favorable opinion of him in 10 of the 15 U.S. surveys in which we have asked about the pope since 2013.

Catholic Democrats (88%) are much more likely than Catholic Republicans (69%) to view Francis favorably.

Note: This is an update of a post originally published Sept. 4, 2018.
